The FT pathway is a technically mature pathway of technology readiness level (TRL) 9 that has been utilized to produce fuels for more than century, originating in Germany during World War I. Today, FT is applied commercially to produce synthetic fuels, notably at large-scale plants in South Africa and Qatar (Sasol n.d.; Shell n.d.). The chemical mechanism of FT involves mixtures of carbon monoxide (CO) and H , a 2 combination known as syngas, that are converted into long, straight-chain hydrocarbons as 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. shown in Eq. 1. This syngas feedstock can be sourced from the deconstruction of a wide variety of carbonaceous feedstocks including coal, natural gas, biomass, municipal wastes, and others. In modern commercial facilities, this is most often accomplished through the reforming of coal or natural gas due to their relatively low cost and wide abundance, whereas future SAF facilities would favor low-carbon-intensity feedstocks. One of the defining characteristics associated with the FT process is the chain growth mechanism and the wide distribution of hydrocarbons produced. Specifically, during the FT reaction the distribution of hydrocarbons is governed by the Anderson-Schulz-Flory probability of chain growth, shown in Figure 9. Depending on the chain growth probability α, the distribution of products can range from almost entirely C in the case of low α values to exclusively high-molecular-weight species 1 >C in the case of high α values. 20 Figure 9. In this range, the yield of hydrocarbons conducive to the most optimal fuel properties (e.g., C –C for SAF) is maximized. 8 16 However, even under these ideal conditions, a range of byproducts is also formed across the light hydrocarbons (e.g., C - C ), gasoline, diesel, and wax ranges.
